books.section: Topic 5.8 Military Conflict in the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Alexander Gardner, Antietam, Maryland: Confederate soldiers, photographed September 1862. Public domain. Image from the shared pool.
stimulus.text: The photograph shows dead Confederate soldiers in gray uniforms lying on the battlefield at Antietam, Maryland, in September 1862. It was taken by Alexander Gardner days after the battle, the first time Americans saw photographs of battlefield dead. Brady exhibited the photographs in New York in October 1862 as “The Dead of Antietam.”

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Antietam is best remembered in the history of the war because it

options.text: gave Lincoln the victory he needed for emancipation.

options.misconception: Background: the war continued until Lee’s surrender in April 1865.

options.text: was the bloodiest battle of the whole war.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Gettysburg was the bloodiest battle overall; Antietam was the bloodiest single day.

options.text: resulted in the capture of Richmond.
options.misconception: Background: Richmond did not fall until April 1865, two and a half years later.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Antietam was enough of a victory for Lincoln to issue the Emancipation Proclamation.
rationales.B: Background: the war continued until Lee’s surrender in April 1865.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Gettysburg was the bloodiest battle overall; Antietam was the bloodiest single day.
rationales.D: Background: Richmond did not fall until April 1865, two and a half years later.
rationales.general:
1. Background from the books: Antietam was not a crushing victory; McClellan turned Lee back but did not destroy his army.
2. What mattered was the timing: Lincoln needed a victory before he could act on slavery.
3. Background from the books: after Antietam, Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation.
4. The battle’s meaning is political, not just military: it changed what the war was about.
Remember: a battle’s importance can be the door it opens, not the ground it takes.
